OK to start off... hybrids vs heirlooms. There's really not a ton of difference if you only care to eat your tomatoes and not save seeds. The main and almost only advantage to heirlooms is when you save the seeds, you get the same plant you grew before. With hybrids you get something that loses traits of its parents, although it'll still grow a probably perfectly fine tomato.

Seedlings. They like to be warm to germinate, I really, really recommend a heating mat to keep the soil temperature 70-80 degrees (up to 85ish should be fine, lower won't really work well). Good to keep light to moderate airflow on them as soon as they sprout. Yes you might have to water twice a day if you have small peat cells, but you might get damping off or worse without airflow. I'll leave lighting research up to you, I've done fine starting stuff in windowsills. If at all possible keep the soil at least 65 (preferably up to 75) degrees while the seedlings are growing or they'll turn purple because they have difficulty taking up phosphorus. They're fine if that happens, they'll just grow very slowly and not survive transplant as well. KEEP THE SEEDLINGS INSIDE/IN A WARM AREA UNTIL YOUR SOIL TEMPERATURE IS 55-60 DEGREES, ABSOLUTE MINIMUM or they'll have a very high death rate at transplant.

Transplant. Not much to learn here, but there are a few things to note. You'll want to bury the tomato plant up to the first true leaves, all the hairs on the stem will turn into roots, so the deeper you bury it, the better chance it'll have to form good roots quickly. DO NOT go past the first true leaves though (true leaves are the ones that will have some kind of texture and unique shape, the "not real" leaves are oval/round and featureless). I honestly don't believe soil matters too much other than make sure it's slightly acidic and isn't going to rot the roots by holding them in a puddle of water.

Actual growing of a mature plant. Copper octanoate (sold as copper fungicide at most garden stores) will save. your. ass. I have never had a tomato plant survive well without it, and that's not my fault, the climate here is basically like living in a fucking ocean. It creates mold, bacterial, and fungal problems to no fucking end. If it's raining more than once every two weeks while growing, you'll want copper fungicide guaranteed. If you find your leaves turning yellow/brown/black, copper fungicide seems to be a cure-all. If you're eager for a big, fast harvest look into "tomato and blossom set spray" although that's not ideal if you don't need it.

Tomato plants need tall support. If plants are determinate, sometimes they'll stop at 3-4 feet, but indeterminate tomatoes will easily grow to 7+ feet over a season, and the best way to keep them healthy in general is to let them grow as tall as they please. Fuck those stupid overpriced 2 foot garden store cages. More here: https://morningchores.com/tomato-trellis-cage/

Tomatoes DO NOT need to ripen fully on the plant. All that's going to get you is a bunch of half eaten tomatoes but the fucking jew slugs and other wildlife that come into your yard. Once the tomato has started turning yellow/orange/whatever, it's OK to pick and there's no advantage to leaving it on the plant. Be careful because some kinds will rip a whole bunch off if you just go yank a tomato right off the plant, I use scissors to cut about a quarter of an inch above the top of the tomato on the stem.

It's never a bad thing to prune off the branches close to the ground that have a chance to touch the ground at any point. Odds are they'll just get soaking wet, rot, and potentially kill your plant, or at the very least any fruit on them will be totally fucking disgusting from insects/mold.

Water at the roots. YOU DO NOT ever want to intentionally get tomato plant leaves/stems wet if you don't absolutely need to. That's what starts bacterial/fungal problems for the most part. I set up a soaker hose this year but you can also just spray on the ground a foot or two away from the plant, that's fine. Consistent medium to light watering is going to reduce your overall problem rate vs waiting until the plant is wilted, or almost so, and soaking the loving fuck out of it.

Fertilizer. this one is up to you, there's little inherently wrong with any kind of fertilizer as long as it's properly balanced. For tomatoes you, at worst, want a balanced fertilizer like 20-20-20, 5-5-5 (as long as the numbers are very close, it's fine, they don't have to be identical), and preferably something a little higher in phosphorous (the third number) than the first two, such as 4-5-6 or 4-4-6 or something. Organic fertilizers are great, but sometimes your plant CAN benefit from something like miracle gro, in limited usage. Organic fertilizers break down as needed but sometimes the soil microbes can't keep up with the plant, so there's nothing wrong with using chemical salts fertilizers if your plant is showing signs of nutrient deficiency or fruit is growing retardedly slow (as in like it takes more than a month for a tomato to mature) but that's rare. Repeated use of fertilizers like miracle gro can leave your soil somewhat toxic, but you really have to overdo it. I personally use 90% organic fertilizer and give a boost with a low dose of miracle grow when the plants look like they're growing way too slowly, but there are many causes of that so I wouldn't just assume without figuring out the cause first.
